A close reading for the week

“A wonderful serenity has taken possession of my entire soul”

Werther · letter of 10 May

On its surface this letter is about lying in long grass on a spring morning. Underneath, it is about a mind so full that it cannot make anything, and the book’s catastrophe is already in its happiest page.

A wonderful serenity has taken possession of my entire soul,1 like these sweet mornings of spring which I enjoy with my whole heart. I am alone, and feel the charm of existence in this spot, which was created for the bliss of souls like mine. I am so happy, my dear friend, so absorbed in the exquisite sense of mere tranquil existence, that I neglect my talents. I should be incapable of drawing a single stroke at the present moment; and yet I feel that I never was a greater artist than now.2

  1. 1

    Possessed by calm

    Serenity has “taken possession” of him: even Werther’s peace is described as a seizure. The verb is the first hint of the book’s pattern. His feelings occupy him, and he never speaks of them as anything but total (“entire soul”, “whole heart”). The letter is happy, but the grammar of being overwhelmed is already in place, waiting for a darker feeling to use it.

  2. 2

    The artist who cannot draw

    At the centre of the letter is a paradox: he could not “draw a single stroke”, yet has never been “a greater artist”. For Werther, art lies in feeling: the fullness of the inner life counts for more than anything it produces. This is the Romantic creed a generation before Wordsworth, and it is also the seed of Werther’s ruin: a man whose feelings need no outlet will, when the feelings turn, have no outlet for them either.
